answers.genai-fm-fundamentals: A foundation model is pretrained at very large scale on broad data, so it learns general representations instead of solving one narrow task. That makes it a shared base you can adapt to many tasks through prompting or fine-tuning, without training from scratch. A traditional model is trained on data for one specific task. Classical models such as XGBoost are still the better choice for structured tabular data, tight latency budgets, low cost, or when you need explainable decisions.
answers.genai-rag-vs-finetuning: Use RAG when the model needs knowledge, especially facts that change often, because you can update documents without retraining. RAG also gives you citations and lets you enforce access controls at retrieval time. Use fine-tuning when you need to change behaviour, such as tone, output format, or a specialised task. Fine-tuned knowledge goes stale and needs retraining. Many production systems combine both: fine-tuning for behaviour and RAG for current facts.
answers.genai-lora-production-serving: LoRA freezes the base model weights and learns each weight update as the product of two small low-rank matrices. Because only those small matrices are trained, the optimizer needs far less memory than full fine-tuning. Adapters can be merged into the base weights so inference has no added latency. To serve many adapters, you keep one shared base model in GPU memory and load or swap adapters per request, which is much cheaper than running a full model copy for each one.
answers.genai-chunking-strategies: Start from the documents and the kinds of questions users ask. Fixed-size chunking is simple but can split ideas apart, while structure-aware chunking follows headings, paragraphs, or code blocks. Size is a trade-off: small chunks match precisely but can lose context, and large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and cost more tokens. A sliding window overlap protects ideas that fall across boundaries. Choose the final settings by measuring retrieval quality on a labelled evaluation set.
answers.genai-dense-vs-sparse-search: Dense vector search captures meaning, so it finds paraphrases even with different words. Sparse keyword search, such as BM25 on an inverted index, is better at exact matches like product codes, names, and rare terms that embeddings can miss. Combining them covers both failure modes. The two result lists use different score scales, so they are commonly merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which combines documents by rank instead of raw score.
answers.genai-rag-reranking-pipeline: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document separately, which is fast but only compares them at the end. A cross-encoder reads the query and document together, so attention can model their interaction, and it scores relevance more accurately. It is too slow to run on the whole corpus, so you use two stages: retrieve a broad candidate set quickly, then rerank those candidates and keep the best few. The trade-off is better precision for extra latency, so you tune the candidate count against your latency budget.
answers.genai-prompt-structured-outputs: The strongest guarantee is constrained decoding, where a grammar or JSON schema masks any token that would make the output invalid. You define the expected structure with a schema, for example using Pydantic, and pass it to the model. You still validate every response in your application, because a valid format can contain wrong values. If validation fails, retry automatically with the error message, with a limit on the number of retries.
answers.genai-prompt-cot-reasoning: Use chain-of-thought for complex tasks that need several steps, such as multi-step maths, logic, or planning. It is rarely worth it for simple lookups or classification. It generates extra tokens, so it adds latency and cost. The written reasoning can also be wrong or may not reflect how the model actually reached its answer, so you should not treat it as proof. Keep the reasoning separate from the final answer, and evaluate whether it actually improves results on your task.
answers.genai-eval-llm-as-judge: Start with an explicit rubric and a clear scoring scale, with examples of each score, instead of asking which answer is better. Judges have known biases, so swap the order of answers to cancel position bias, and control for verbosity bias, where longer answers get higher scores. Avoid self-preference by using a judge from a different model family than the one being tested. Finally, calibrate the judge against a human-labelled set and track agreement over time.
answers.genai-eval-rag-triad-hallucination: The RAG Triad checks three links. Faithfulness, or groundedness, asks whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, and this is the direct check for hallucination. Context relevance asks whether the retrieved passages are relevant to the question, which tests the retriever. Answer relevance asks whether the answer actually addresses the question. Scoring all three separately tells you whether a failure came from retrieval or from generation.
answers.genai-hallucination-mitigation: Prevention starts with grounding: instruct the model to answer only from provided context, require citations, and allow it to say it does not know. For factual tasks, lower the temperature to reduce random output. To intercept errors, sample several answers and check whether they agree, because disagreement is a useful warning sign. You can also verify claims against sources with a separate check, and route high-risk or low-confidence answers to a person.
answers.genai-agent-react-tool-calling: A ReAct agent repeats a cycle of thought, action, and observation. The model reasons about what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and continues until it can answer. Tools are defined with clear schemas, and their calls are parsed and validated before they run. To prevent runaway loops, enforce a maximum number of steps, plus time and cost budgets. Also detect repeated identical calls and break the cycle, then stop gracefully or hand off to a person.
answers.genai-agent-single-vs-multi: Start with one agent, and add more only when you have a real need. Multi-agent designs help when one agent has too many tools to choose from accurately, or when unrelated context pollutes its prompt. A common pattern is a supervisor that routes work to specialised agents, each with a small tool set and focused context. The cost is that every extra agent adds model calls, latency, and new ways to fail, so measure whether quality improves enough to justify it.
answers.genai-guardrails-prompt-injection-pii: Treat all outside text as untrusted data, not as instructions. Separate it from system instructions with clear delimiters, and remember that this reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Indirect injection can arrive through retrieved documents or web pages, so sanitise that content and give tools the least privilege possible, with approval for risky actions. Add classifiers before and after the model to catch attacks and unsafe output, and detect and redact personal data on both input and output.
answers.genai-cost-latency-ttft-tpot: Time to first token mostly reflects queueing plus the prefill phase that processes the prompt. Time per output token reflects the decode phase, which generates tokens one at a time. Measure them separately, using percentiles and not just averages. To reduce time to first token, shorten prompts and use prompt caching so a shared prefix reuses its KV cache. To reduce time per output token, use efficient batching, quantization, or a smaller model. Streaming tokens as they are generated also makes the response feel faster.
answers.genai-serving-kv-cache-pagedattention: During generation, the model keeps the key and value tensors for every previous token in every layer, so that it does not have to recompute them. This KV cache grows with each token and each concurrent request, which often makes it the main GPU memory limit. Allocating contiguous memory for the maximum length wastes space and causes fragmentation. PagedAttention splits the cache into small fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like virtual memory pages, so more requests fit and throughput rises. It can also share blocks between requests with a common prefix.
answers.genai-serving-quantization: Weight-only quantization compresses just the stored weights, which reduces size and memory with a simple process, and is common for GPU serving. Weight-activation quantization also quantizes activations at runtime. It can reduce computation further, but activations contain outliers that hurt accuracy if they are quantized naively. Methods such as SmoothQuant and AWQ handle this by protecting the salient weights and channels. Smaller models also need less memory bandwidth, which speeds up inference, so always measure accuracy against your speed gain.
answers.genai-finetuning-alignment-dpo-rlhf: Traditional RLHF requires several stages: train a reward model on preference data, then optimise the policy with reinforcement learning such as PPO. That process is complex and can be unstable. DPO uses the same preference pairs but derives a direct loss, with an implicit reward defined relative to a reference model. It needs no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop, so it is simpler, more stable, and cheaper to train. You still need high quality preference data, and results depend on the task.
answers.genai-finetuning-data-curation-forgettin: Prioritise quality over quantity: a smaller set of clean, representative, expert-checked examples usually beats a large noisy one. Deduplicate data, remove low quality or contaminated examples, and keep train and test sets strictly separate so scores stay honest. To limit catastrophic forgetting, where new training erodes earlier abilities, mix in a portion of general or previous examples during training. Then evaluate on both the new task and older capabilities to catch regressions.
answers.genai-rag-advanced-query-expansion: HyDE asks an LLM to write a hypothetical answer to the query, then embeds that text for retrieval instead of the short query. This works because an answer-like passage sits closer to real documents in embedding space, which bridges the gap between short questions and long documents. Query expansion instead decomposes or rewrites a question into several sub-queries, retrieves for each, and merges the results. The trade-offs are additional latency and cost, and a badly generated hypothesis can pull in the wrong documents.
